title: What is an algorithm?
summary: Recipes for computers, and how we measure their speed.

cards.title: A recipe for a computer
cards.body:
An **algorithm** is a list of steps that solves a problem, like a recipe.

Your game has 1,000,000 players. Someone types a name. How do you find that player? The steps you choose decide whether it takes a blink or a coffee break.

cards.title: The simplest idea
cards.body:
Check every player, one by one, from the start. Stop when you find the name.

This is **linear search**. It always works, but it can be slow. Watch it on a small list.
Press play. Each step checks one box.

cards.title: Count the steps, not the seconds
cards.body:
Phones get faster every year, so we don't measure algorithms in seconds. We **count steps**.

- 5 players: up to 5 checks.
- 1,000 players: up to 1,000 checks.
- n players: up to **n** checks.

When steps grow in step with n, we write **O(n)** and say "order n". This is **Big-O notation**: it describes how the work grows as the input grows.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body:
An O(n) search over 1,000,000 players can take 1,000,000 checks.

In a few lessons you will learn **binary search**, which needs only about 20 checks for the same list. Same computer, same data, about 50,000 times less work. Choosing the algorithm is the real optimisation.

cards.question: Linear search looks for a name in a list of 400 players. The name is **not** in the list. How many checks does it make?
cards.explain: It has to look at every player before it can be sure the name is missing: 400 checks. That's the **worst case**, and Big-O usually describes the worst case.

cards.question: List A has 10 items, list B has 10,000. Linear search on B does at most how many times more checks than on A?
cards.explain: 10,000 / 10 = 1,000. With O(n), work grows **in proportion** to the input.
